title: Self-Hosted Git with Forgejo on Unraid

sections.heading: Architecture Overview
content: This guide covers deploying a self-hosted Forgejo instance on Unraid with a PostgreSQL backend, fronted by Nginx Proxy Manager for secure external access via a custom subdomain.

Forgejo is a community-hardened fork of Gitea, providing a lightweight, self-contained Git server with issues, pull requests, CI/CD (Forgejo Actions), and a full API compatible with Gitea's tooling. The official CLI is tea (originally Gitea's CLI), which works identically with Forgejo.

Why self-host git instead of using GitHub? The primary motivation for this migration was GitHub's Terms of Service, which limit free accounts to a single machine user per personal account. In a multi-agent setup where each agent needs its own Git identity, this cap is quickly reached. Self-hosting removes the limit entirely — you can create as many users as your infrastructure needs.
Traffic flow: Git client → Cloudflare (proxy) → Nginx Proxy Manager → Forgejo container (port 3003) → PostgreSQL database.

Agent tooling: Each agent uses tea CLI (v0.15.1) for Git operations and a forgejo-api wrapper script for direct API calls (reviews, comments, diffs). Git authentication is handled transparently via tea login helper as a git credential helper.

sections.heading: Prerequisites
content: Before starting, confirm the following:
• A Unraid server with Docker and Docker Compose available
• Nginx Proxy Manager already running (or follow the reverse proxy guide to set it up first)
• A domain with Cloudflare DNS pointing to your server (wildcard A record recommended)
• A ready-to-use subdomain (e.g. git.yourdomain.com)
• Basic familiarity with the Unraid terminal or SSH access to the server

sections.heading: Phase 1: Deploy Forgejo + PostgreSQL
sections.subtitle: Forgejo runs as a Docker container with a companion PostgreSQL database. A separate .env file stores the database password.
steps: Create the data directories: SSH into your Unraid server and create the Forgejo data directory structure:
mkdir -p /mnt/user/appdata/forgejo/data
mkdir -p /mnt/user/appdata/forgejo/database
Create the .env file:
nano /mnt/user/appdata/forgejo/.env
Paste the following, replacing the password with a strong value:
Create the Docker Compose file:
nano /mnt/user/appdata/forgejo/docker-compose.yml
Paste the following compose file:

steps.code:
networks:
  forgejo:
    external: false

services:
  server:
    image: codeberg.org/forgejo/forgejo:16
    container_name: forgejo
    restart: always
    networks:
      - forgejo
    ports:
      - '3003:3000'
    volumes:
      - /mnt/user/appdata/forgejo/data:/data
      - /etc/localtime:/etc/localtime:ro
    environment:
      - USER_UID=1000
      - USER_GID=1000
      - TZ=America/New_York
      - FORGEJO__database__DB_TYPE=postgres
      - FORGEJO__database__HOST=database:5432
      - FORGEJO__database__NAME=forgejo
      - FORGEJO__database__USER=forgejo
      - FORGEJO__database__PASSWD=${FORGEJO_DATABASE_PASSWORD}
      - FORGEJO__server__DOMAIN=git.yourdomain.com
      - FORGEJO__server__ROOT_URL=https://git.yourdomain.com
      - FORGEJO__server__HTTP_PORT=3000
    depends_on:
      database:
        condition: service_healthy

  database:
    image: postgres:17
    container_name: forgejo-database
    restart: always
    networks:
      - forgejo
    volumes:
      - /mnt/user/appdata/forgejo/database:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    environment:
      - POSTGRES_DB=forgejo
      - POSTGRES_USER=forgejo
      - POSTGRES_PASSWORD=${FORGEJO_DATABASE_PASSWORD}
    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD-SHELL", "pg_isready -U forgejo"]
      interval: 5s
      timeout: 5s
      retries: 5

steps: The key environment variables configure Forgejo to connect to the PostgreSQL container. The depends_on with condition: service_healthy ensures Forgejo waits for PostgreSQL to be fully ready before starting — this prevents the crashloop that occurs when Forgejo starts before the database is initialized.
Start the stack:
cd /mnt/user/appdata/forgejo && docker compose up -d
Forgejo will be accessible at http://YOUR_SERVER_IP:3003. The initial setup wizard should have the database fields pre-populated from the environment variables.

sections.heading: Phase 2: Initial Setup Wizard
sections.subtitle: Access Forgejo directly via its LAN IP and port, then configure the instance through the web UI.
steps: Open http://YOUR_SERVER_IP:3003 in a browser. You should see the Forgejo setup wizard with the database fields already filled in from the environment variables.
Under General Settings:
• Instance Title: choose something meaningful (e.g. Harrsch-Industries)
• Server Domain: git.yourdomain.com
• Base URL: https://git.yourdomain.com
• Disable self-registration: true (recommended)
Under Server and Third-Party Service Settings (Optional settings):
• Disable OpenID sign-in: false
• Require sign-in to view content: true (recommended for private server)
• Allow creation of organizations by default: false (recommended)
Under Administrator Account Settings:
• Create an admin account. A two-account approach is recommended: one admin user for instance management, and a separate personal user for daily work.
Click Install Forgejo. The setup may take 30–60 seconds as it creates the database tables. Do not refresh the page during this time.
After installation, log in and create your organization (e.g. Harrsch-Industries) via the top-right avatar → Dashboard → Organizations → New Organization.

Note: Accessing the setup wizard via the LAN IP after the domain is configured may cause a redirect loop. Always use the configured domain (e.g. https://git.yourdomain.com) for the initial setup if possible. If you must use the LAN IP, temporarily remove the ROOT_URL and DOMAIN environment variables, complete the wizard, then add them back.

sections.heading: Phase 3: Configure Nginx Proxy Manager
sections.subtitle: Expose Forgejo through NPM for secure external access with automatic SSL.
steps: In Nginx Proxy Manager → Proxy Hosts → Add Proxy Host.
Domain Names: git.yourdomain.com.
Scheme: http.
Forward Hostname/IP: your Unraid server's LAN IP.
Forward Port: 3003.
Toggle Block Common Exploits → on.
SSL tab → select your wildcard cert → toggle Force SSL and HTTP/2 Support → Save.
Ensure the Cloudflare DNS entry for git.yourdomain.com exists and is proxied (orange cloud).
Test by visiting https://git.yourdomain.com — you should see the Forgejo login page.

sections.heading: Phase 4: Create Users and Organizations
sections.subtitle: Create machine users for each agent and add them to the organization with appropriate permissions.
steps: In Forgejo → Site Administration (top-right avatar) → Identity & Access → User Accounts → Create User Account.
Create a user for each autonomous agent: hi-pm-agent, hi-eng-agent, hi-devops-agent, hi-security-agent.
Use the email convention harrsch.agents+@gmail.com (or your own pattern).
For each user, create a personal access token: Settings → Applications → Generate Token with scopes: write:repository, write:issue, read:user, read:admin.
In the organization → Teams → create an agents team with admin permissions on all repositories, and add all machine users to it.
Alternatively, use the Forgejo API from an admin account to create users, tokens, and team memberships programmatically:

steps.code:
# Add user to team
curl -X PUT -H "Authorization: token <ADMIN_PAT>" \
  "https://git.yourdomain.com/api/v1/teams/<TEAM_ID>/members/<USERNAME>"

# Create PAT for user
curl -X POST -H "Authorization: token <ADMIN_PAT>" \
  -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
  -d '{"name":"hermes-agent","scopes":["write:repository","write:issue","read:user","read:admin"]}' \
  "https://git.yourdomain.com/api/v1/admin/users/<USERNAME>/tokens"

sections.heading: Phase 5: Configure Agent Tooling
sections.subtitle: Install the tea CLI and set up git credential helpers on each agent VM.
steps: Install the tea CLI on each agent's Linux user:
sudo -u <agent> curl -sL 'https://gitea.com/gitea/tea/releases/download/v0.15.1/tea-0.15.1-linux-amd64' -o ~agent/.local/bin/tea
sudo -u <agent> chmod +x ~agent/.local/bin/tea
Create the forgejo-api helper script (wraps curl with auth from the FORGEJO_TOKEN environment variable, avoiding inline credential exposure in cron prompts):

steps.code:
#!/bin/bash
CURL="/usr/bin/curl"
METHOD="$1"
API_PATH="$2"
BODY="$3"
BASE_URL="https://git.yourdomain.com/api/v1"

if [ "$METHOD" = "GET" ]; then
  $CURL -sf -H "Authorization: token $FORGEJO_TOKEN" "$BASE_URL$API_PATH"
elif [ "$METHOD" = "POST" ] && [ -n "$BODY" ]; then
  $CURL -sf -X POST -H "Authorization: token $FORGEJO_TOKEN" -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d "$BODY" "$BASE_URL$API_PATH"
elif [ "$METHOD" = "POST" ]; then
  $CURL -sf -X POST -H "Authorization: token $FORGEJO_TOKEN" "$BASE_URL$API_PATH"
else
  echo "Usage: forgejo-api GET|POST /path [body]"
  exit 1
fi

steps: Log in with tea:
tea login add --name forgejo --url https://git.yourdomain.com --token <PAT>
Register the git credential helper so git push and git clone authenticate transparently:
tea logins helper setup
Then fix the helper to use the absolute path (since ~/.local/bin may not be in PATH):
git config --global --replace-all credential.https://git.yourdomain.com.helper "!/home/<agent>/.local/bin/tea logins helper"
Add the PAT to the agent's environment:
echo 'FORGEJO_TOKEN=<PAT>' >> ~agent/.hermes/.env
Update git remotes on any existing cloned repos to point to Forgejo:
git remote set-url origin https://git.yourdomain.com/ORG/REPO.git

sections.heading: Phase 6: Migrate Repos from GitHub
sections.subtitle: Clone existing repos from GitHub as mirrors and push them to Forgejo. This preserves the full commit history, all branches, and all tags. Issues and PRs are not migrated — they are recreated in Forgejo as needed.
steps: For each repo to migrate, create an empty repo in Forgejo first via the API or web UI, then mirror-push:
git clone --mirror https://github.com/ORG/REPO.git
cd REPO.git
git push --mirror https://git.yourdomain.com/ORG/REPO.git
After migration, add the FORGEJO_TOKEN to each agent's .env file and update the GITHUB_TOKEN reference in cron prompts to use tea and forgejo-api instead of gh.

sections.heading: Phase 7: Event Webhooks and Branch Protection
sections.subtitle: Wire Forgejo's own webhooks to a local receiver, then lock the default branch so changes can only arrive as pull requests.
steps: Forgejo can announce its own events — no CI workflow required. An organization webhook covers every repo in the org, including repos you create later. Organization → Settings → Webhooks → Add Webhook → Forgejo. (A per-repo agent-trigger.yml workflow that re-posts events by hand is the redundant version of this; it also means every new repo starts deaf until someone remembers to copy the file in.)

Target: POST, content type application/json, URL http://<receiver-host>:<port>/webhook. Set Trigger On → Custom events and tick Issues and Pull requests, including their sub-events — Assignment and Review requested are tracked as separate flags from the parent category.

Gotcha 1 — a webhook saved with nothing ticked. Under Custom events with no boxes checked, the hook is active, appears configured in the UI, and delivers nothing. Every event flag reads false in the database. Check the flags, not the page.
Gotcha 2 — SSRF protection blocks your own LAN. Forgejo will not call a private address until you allowlist it. In app.ini:

[webhook]
  ALLOWED_HOST_LIST = <receiver-host>

Use the exact host, not *. The guarded failure looks like nothing happened: the delivery row reads is_succeed=false, status 0, with a body naming the deny — and nothing at all appears in the receiver's log, because no connection was ever attempted.

Gotcha 3 — the event header was renamed. Forgejo sends X-Forgejo-Event and X-GitHub-Event. It does not send X-Gitea-Event. A receiver keyed only to the old Gitea name answers 400 missing event type and every event dies quietly. Accept all three header names.

Test the pipe without waking an agent. Comment on an issue and watch the delivery: a receiver that logs Received issue_comment and then ignores it proves transport end to end. Save real agent-firing tests for genuine work.
Protect the default branch before agents can write to it. Settings → Branches → Add Rule, or via the API:

enable_push=false — direct pushes refused
required_approvals=1 — one review before merge
dismiss_stale_approvals=true — new commits void the old approval
block_on_outdated_branch=true — rebase instead of merging main into the branch
block_on_rejected_reviews=true — a "changes requested" review blocks merge

Verify it actually bites. Attempt a direct write with your own repo-admin token — if it succeeds, the protection is applied to the wrong branch or you are a site admin. The expected answer is 403 user cannot commit to repo.

Then retire the workarounds. Once the org webhook delivers issue and PR events, delete the per-repo agent-trigger.yml files. Keep any workflow that runs a job Actions must execute — deploys, for instance, are not an event Forgejo can webhook.

sections.heading: tea CLI Reference
content: The tea CLI is the official Gitea/Forgejo command-line tool. Key commands for agent automation:
<table><thead><tr><th>Action</th><th>Command</th></tr></thead><tbody>
List PRs (org-wide)tea issues list --login forgejo --owner ORG --kind pulls --state open --output json
List issues (assigned)tea issues list --login forgejo --owner ORG --assignee USER --state open --output json
View PR diffforgejo-api GET /repos/ORG/REPO/pulls/N.diff
Submit reviewforgejo-api POST /repos/ORG/REPO/pulls/N/reviews '{"event":"APPROVED|REQUEST_CHANGES","body":"..."}'
Merge PRtea pulls merge N --repo ORG/REPO --style squash --login forgejo
Add reviewertea pulls edit N --repo ORG/REPO --add-reviewers USER --login forgejo
Create issuetea issues create --repo ORG/REPO --title "..." --login forgejo
Comment on PRforgejo-api POST /repos/ORG/REPO/issues/N/comments '{"body":"..."}'
Create PRtea pulls create --repo ORG/REPO --base main --head BRANCH --title "..." --login forgejo
Checkout PRgit fetch origin && git checkout BRANCH

sections.heading: Changelog
sections.subtitle: What changed, and when.
content: 2026-10-30v1Event webhooks and branch protectionFirst recorded revision. Adds Phase 7: an organization webhook pointed at a local receiver, the three silent failure modes (no events ticked, an SSRF allowlist that refuses private addresses, and a receiver reading the retired X-Gitea-Event header), and the branch-protection settings that make main accept changes only through reviewed pull requests. Earlier revisions of this guide predate the changelog.
